ZHIWHIS ZWS-A330 Review

Share this review:hqshortwaveradio.com/reviews/zhiwhis-zws-a330/
★★★★☆4.0/5✓ Hands-On Tested — Not a Spec-Sheet Review

A shirt-pocket radio that covers almost everything: AM, FM, shortwave with SSB, air band, CB, NOAA weather with alerts, and wide VHF/UHF. It adds recording, Bluetooth, app control and USB-C charging. It's built to go wherever you go: outdoors, in the truck, or in a go-bag.

Specifications

BandsMW 520–1710 kHz · SW 2.3–30 MHz · FM 64–108 MHz · Air 118–138 MHz · CB 25–28 MHz · VHF 20–250 MHz · UHF to 999 MHz · NOAA WB 162.400–162.550 MHz
Long wave153–522 kHz, only with the optional ZWS-W3 signal repeater
ModesAM, FM, NFM and SSB (USB/LSB)
BandwidthSW AM: 1, 1.8, 2, 2.5, 3, 4 and 6 kHz · SSB: 0.5, 1, 1.2, 2.2, 3 and 4 kHz
TuningKeypad entry, tuning knob, up/down scan, ATS auto-store, presets, SW meter-band shortcuts
Squelch / ATT9-level squelch on SW, VHF, UHF, Air and CB · Local/DX attenuator
WeatherNOAA weather band with alert function
Recording & mediaRecords to microSD (up to 256 GB) with date, time and frequency in the file name · MP3/WMA/WAV/APE/FLAC playback
ConnectivityBluetooth speaker, app control, USB computer speaker, headphone jack
AntennaThin telescopic whip · 3.5 mm external antenna jack · plug-in loop antenna for MW included
PowerBL-5C removable lithium battery · USB-C charging
SizeAbout 136 × 60 × 35 mm, shirt-pocket size
In the boxRadio, belt clip (factory-fitted), wrist strap, MW loop antenna, screwdriver, manual

Pros

  • Pocket-size with full-size coverage: shortwave, SSB, air band, CB, NOAA weather and VHF/UHF in a radio that slips into a shirt pocket. Few radios this small cover this much.
  • Made for outdoors and portable use: light, one-handed operation (every control is on the front, top and right side), and it stands upright on its own on a picnic table or tailgate
  • A strong prepper and go-bag radio: NOAA weather with alerts, AM/FM news, shortwave for news from outside the area, and air band and VHF/UHF scanning, all on one rechargeable radio
  • The BL-5C battery is a common, cheap, swappable cell. Carry a spare in the bag and you're not stuck waiting on a charger, and USB-C charging works from a power bank or solar panel
  • Shortwave delivered on the band scan from San Tan Valley, AZ: WRMI on 5850 kHz (Florida, 1,860 mi), WWCR on 5935 kHz (Tennessee, 1,410 mi), Radio Martí on 6030 kHz (North Carolina, 1,950 mi) and China Radio International on 15160 kHz from Jinhua, China, about 7,030 miles away
  • AM (MW) DX surprised me: with the plug-in ferrite rod antenna, after midnight from San Tan Valley I logged KNBR 680 San Francisco (673 mi), KSL 1160 Salt Lake City (525 mi) and KOKC 1520 Oklahoma City (814 mi), plus KFYI 550 and KNST 790 locally. You can rotate the rod to peak a station and narrow the bandwidth from 3.0 to 2.0 kHz to split shared channels like 740 kHz.
  • Real SSB with six bandwidth choices, so you can listen to ham radio nets on 40 m and 80 m and to utility stations, not just broadcast AM
  • Air band is excellent: tower and pilot audio comes through crystal clear and easy to understand, even off the stock antenna. The 9-level squelch keeps it silent between transmissions, so it's a fantastic airport-fence, airshow or hiking radio
  • Plenty of loud, clear audio from the small speaker, easy to hear at a campsite or over wind
  • Records what you hear to microSD with the date, time and frequency in the file name, which is handy for logging catches or saving an emergency broadcast
  • Bluetooth, app control and USB speaker mode make it double as a music player and phone/PC speaker on a trip
  • The 3.5 mm external antenna jack means a simple clip-on wire can boost shortwave in the field

Cons

  • The telescopic antenna is very thin. It feels fragile and will bend if it catches on a bag strap or a branch, so handle it with care and collapse it before packing. For heavy outdoor use, plan on a clip-on wire antenna through the 3.5 mm jack.
  • The holster/belt clip isn't great. It's bulky, adds thickness, and sits over the battery door, which gets in the way when you swap the BL-5C. Its hold isn't confidence-inspiring for hiking. A small padded pouch protects the radio and antenna better.
  • On shortwave it's a solid performer, but dedicated portables like the Tecsun PL-330 still pull in weak stations it misses
  • The screen is hard to read in some outdoor light, and it isn't readable at all with the backlight off
  • The buttons are small and stiff, and the tuning knob is a little stiff too, which is awkward with gloves on
  • Settings share buttons with frequency entry, so it's easy to change something by accident, and the settings text on screen is tiny
  • The CB band can't step in 10 kHz channels, so manual tuning across CB is slow
  • No flashlight or kickstand, two features a lot of outdoor and prepper radios include
  • Long wave only works with the extra-cost W3 repeater

Verdict

The ZHIWHIS ZWS-A330 is the kind of radio you actually take with you. It's small enough for a shirt pocket or the side pouch of a backpack, yet it covers AM, FM, shortwave with SSB, air band, CB, NOAA weather and wide VHF/UHF. My band scan from San Tan Valley pulled in WRMI, WWCR, Radio Martí and China Radio International on shortwave. On AM, the plug-in ferrite rod turned it into a real nighttime DX machine: San Francisco, Salt Lake City and Oklahoma City, up to 814 miles away, after midnight. That range of coverage and performance in such a small package is the A330's real strength.

For outdoors and portable listening it hits the right notes: one-handed controls, a loud speaker, recording to microSD, and a swappable BL-5C battery that charges over USB-C. For preppers, it's an easy pick for the go-bag. One rechargeable radio gives you NOAA weather alerts, local AM/FM news, shortwave news from outside the area, and air band and VHF/UHF to hear what's going on nearby. Air band in particular is a standout: excellent, clear and easy to follow. Toss in a spare BL-5C and a short wire antenna, and you're covered.

It isn't perfect. The telescopic antenna is thin and needs gentle handling, and the belt clip/holster is the weakest part of the package: bulky, in the way of the battery door, and not something I'd trust on a hike. The screen washes out in some outdoor light, and dedicated shortwave portables still dig out weaker signals. But as an all-in-one portable and prepper radio, it earns its place. Rating: 4/5.

Hands-on review by Michael Smith / KM7FMJ at ShortwaveHQ, including a shortwave band scan from San Tan Valley, AZ (Sept 27, 2026, 0200 UTC) and an overnight AM (MW) DX session with the plug-in ferrite rod antenna (Oct 18, 2026, 12:30–12:51 AM MST).
